title: New roles in Orthodoxy
hookLine: women scholars and leaders in Orthodox settings; the debates continue

cards: The Talmud tells of a scholar named Rabbi Meir, troubled by some neighbors who made his life miserable. He prayed that they would die. His wife Beruriah stopped him.
Read the psalm again, she said. It asks that sins be ended, not sinners. Pray that they turn back, and then there will be no more wicked people.
Rabbi Meir prayed that way, the story says, and they turned. In the pages of the Talmud, a woman corrects a great sage's reading of a verse, and he listens.

teach.b: New roles in Orthodoxy. Back on day one thousand forty-one, you met women rabbis and the Orthodox debate. Today, up close.
First, the old voices. The Bible names women who taught and judged: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time."

When the scroll of the law was found in the Temple, the king's men went to consult "Huldah the prophetess." And there's Beruriah, a teacher of Torah in the Talmud's own pages. Second, the new study halls.
In recent generations, Orthodox women have taken up deep study of Talmud and halakha in their own study halls, and some now teach it at a high level. Third, new roles.
One is the yoetzet halakha, a woman trained to advise on the laws of family and marriage that touch very private parts of life, so that women can ask a woman.
Others serve congregations as scholars, teachers or spiritual leaders, under titles some communities have chosen carefully.

teach.h: A REAL DEBATE, INSIDE THE LAW.
teach.b: Fourth, the debate, and it's a real one. Some Orthodox rabbis and bodies welcome these roles as faithful to halakha.

teach.h: SHE JUDGED ISRAEL AT THAT TIME.
teach.b: Others hold that certain roles, especially the title rabbi, cross a line that tradition has kept, and say so firmly. Both sides argue from the same law and say they are protecting it. This lesson doesn't settle it.
The argument is happening inside Orthodoxy, among people who hold halakha binding, which is why it matters so much to them. Beruriah's story is still taught in their study halls.
What it means for today is exactly what they debate.

how: In some Orthodox communities, women study Talmud and halakha at advanced levels, serve as yoatzot halakha advising on family law, and hold teaching or leadership roles, while other Orthodox authorities oppose some of these roles.

games.q: you're Rabbi Meir, and your neighbors have made your life miserable. you start to pray they die. Beruriah stops you. what does she say?
o: pray that their sins end, so they turn back.
games.why: she reads the psalm as asking for an end to sins, not sinners. he prays that way, the story says, and they turn.

practice: Bring back the yoetzet halakha, a woman someone can ask a private question of, quietly, and get an answer from the law.

Then think of a role in your own world that someone stepped into for the first time, maybe your mother, a teacher, you: what did it cost them, and what did it open? Hold it gently, without deciding anything.

wordCard.voice: New roles in Orthodoxy. Women as scholars, advisers and leaders in Orthodox settings, from the yoetzet halakha to teachers of Talmud, and a debate about them that continues. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a woman who advises on halakha, one of the new roles in Orthodox communities.
